metadata.description: Multiple-choice questions organized by topics and chapters.

questions.question: Which of the following is wrong about tonsils?

options.A: The tonsil is innervated by branches from the glossopharyngeal nerve
options.B: Upper pole supply by ascending pharyngeal artery
options.C: Lymphatic drainage includes the upper jugular and jugulodigastric lymph nodes

questions.explanation: Statement B is WRONG (false) regarding palatine tonsil anatomy: the arterial supply to the UPPER pole of the tonsil is derived from the ascending palatine artery and lesser palatine artery, while the ascending pharyngeal artery supplies the LOWER pole along with the tonsillar branch of the facial artery and dorsal lingual artery. The tonsil is innervated sensory-wise by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) and drains primarily to the jugulodigastric (tonsillar) lymph node. High-yield pearl: Tonsil Arterial Supply: Lower pole (Main supply) = Tonsillar branch of Facial artery (largest), Ascending pharyngeal, Dorsal lingual. Upper pole = Ascending palatine, Lesser palatine. Nerve = Glossopharyngeal (CN IX). Exam trap: Referred otalgia after tonsillectomy or in tonsillitis is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via Jacobson's tympanic branch. [Source note - suspected source error: commonly cited anatomy references place the ascending pharyngeal artery at the upper pole and the ascending palatine artery at the lower pole, the reverse of this source's assignment. The source key is retained; please verify against your course text.]

optionExplanations.A: True: The tonsillar plexus is innervated by branches from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), explaining referred otalgia.
optionExplanations.B: Correct (this is the false statement). Per the source, the ascending pharyngeal artery supplies the lower pole; the upper pole is supplied by the ascending palatine and lesser palatine arteries.
optionExplanations.C: True: Primary lymphatic drainage is to the jugulodigastric (subdigastric) node of Level II.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the arterial and sensory nerve anatomy of the palatine tonsils.

questions.question: An absolute indication for tonsillectomy is:
questions.explanation: Indications for tonsillectomy are strictly stratified: ABSOLUTE indications include: 1) Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) with cor pulmonale, growth failure, or severe daytime somnolence; 2) Suspected malignant neoplasm (e.g., asymmetric tonsillar hypertrophy); and 3) Uncontrolled or recurrent hemorrhagic tonsillitis. In contrast, peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is a RELATIVE indication (often managed with needle aspiration/incision and drainage, reserving 'quinsy tonsillectomy' for recurrent abscess or children unable to tolerate drainage). High-yield pearl: Tonsillectomy Indications: Absolute: Severe OSA, Asymmetric tonsil (suspected malignancy), Uncontrolled hemorrhage. Relative: Recurrent bacterial tonsillitis (Paradise criteria: 7 episodes in 1 yr, 5/yr for 2 yrs, 3/yr for 3 yrs), Peritonsillar abscess. Exam trap: A single episode of peritonsillar abscess is NOT an absolute indication for immediate tonsillectomy; needle aspiration plus antibiotics is initial standard of care. [Source note: only option A is displayed in the source, but its analysis also discusses options B and C, which are not shown.]

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Obstructive sleep apnea is an absolute indication for tonsillectomy.

questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate absolute indications for tonsillectomy (OSA, suspected malignancy, severe hemorrhage) from relative indications.

questions.question: Not true about tonsillitis:
questions.explanation: Acute tonsillitis typically presents with severe odynophagia, high fever, anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, headache, malaise, and nausea/vomiting (especially in children). In contrast, COUGH is characteristically ABSENT; the presence of prominent cough, rhinorrhea, hoarseness, and conjunctivitis strongly points to a viral upper respiratory infection rather than primary acute tonsillitis (as codified in the Centor criteria). High-yield pearl: Centor Criteria for Streptococcal Pharyngitis: 1) Fever (>38°C); 2) Tonsillar exudates; 3) Tender anterior cervical LAD; 4) Absence of COUGH. Presence of cough suggests a viral URI! Exam trap: If a patient has sore throat with prominent cough and coryza, think viral infection; avoid indiscriminate antibiotic prescribing.

optionExplanations.A: Nausea and abdominal pain are common systemic features of streptococcal tonsillitis in children.
optionExplanations.B: Headache is a classic systemic manifestation of acute tonsillitis.
optionExplanations.C: Correct (not true of tonsillitis). Cough is characteristically absent; a prominent cough points to a viral upper respiratory infection.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall that cough is absent in classic streptococcal tonsillitis and serves as a negative predictor on Centor scoring.

questions.question: Trismus caused by spasm in peritonsillar abscess involves which muscle?
questions.explanation: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is a collection of pus between the tonsillar capsule and the superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle. A hallmark physical sign is severe trismus (inability to open the mouth). This trismus is caused by inflammatory irritation, edema, and reflex spasm of the MEDIAL PTERYGOID MUSCLE, which lies immediately lateral to the superior constrictor muscle in the parapharyngeal space. High-yield pearl: Peritonsillar Abscess (Quinsy): Trismus (medial pterygoid spasm) + 'Hot potato' muffled voice + Uvula deviation to the CONTRALATERAL side + Superior-lateral tonsillar bulge. Treatment: Needle aspiration or I&D + IV/oral antibiotics. Exam trap: Severe trismus in a patient with sore throat indicates infection has spread beyond the tonsil into the peritonsillar space or parapharyngeal space.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Inflammation and reflex spasm of the medial pterygoid muscle, which lies lateral to the superior constrictor, produce the trismus.
optionExplanations.B: The superior pharyngeal constrictor forms the bed of the tonsil, but the masticatory muscle responsible for jaw closure and trismus is the medial pterygoid muscle.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify spasm of the medial pterygoid muscle as the anatomical cause of trismus in peritonsillar abscess.

questions.question: Mononucleosis is associated with:
questions.explanation: Infectious mononucleosis caused by EBV is classically associated with symmetric cervical lymphadenopathy (predominantly posterior cervical chain), exudative pharyngitis, and lifelong persistence of antibodies to EBV (viral capsid antigen VCA-IgG and nuclear antigen EBNA). Thrombocytosis is NOT typical; mild transient thrombocytopenia occurs in ~50% of patients. High-yield pearl: Mononucleosis Triad: Fever + Pharyngitis + Posterior Cervical Lymphadenopathy. Peripheral smear shows atypical CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (Downey cells). Exam trap: Posterior cervical lymphadenopathy favors mononucleosis; anterior cervical lymphadenopathy favors streptococcal pharyngitis. [Source note: option B (lifelong antibodies to EBV) is also true according to the source rationale; the source key (C) is retained.]

optionExplanations.A: Thrombocytopenia (not thrombocytosis) occurs in mononucleosis due to splenic sequestration or immune destruction.
optionExplanations.B: Lifelong antibodies to EBV develop, but lymphadenopathy is the primary physical sign testing clinical recognition here.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Symmetric cervical (predominantly posterior chain) lymphadenopathy is a core feature of infectious mononucleosis.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize lymphadenopathy as a core clinical manifestation of infectious mononucleosis.

questions.question: Which statement is false about obstructive sleep apnea?

options.A: Decreases the risk of motor vehicle accidents

questions.explanation: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is caused by repetitive collapse of the pharyngeal airway during sleep. It causes intermittent hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and frequent micro-arousals that severely fragment sleep architecture, drastically impairing and reducing restorative slow-wave and REM sleep. Severe daytime hypersomnolence markedly INCREASES the risk of motor vehicle collisions (by 2-to 7-fold). Male sex and obesity are major risk factors; female sex is NOT a risk factor (pre-menopausal females have lower prevalence due to progesterone airway protection). High-yield pearl: Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Repetitive pharyngeal collapse -> intermittent hypoxia -> systemic hypertension, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, polycythemia. In children: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is the #1 cause (cured by adenotonsillectomy). Exam trap: In children with OSA, sleepiness may manifest paradoxically as hyperactivity, behavioral problems, and failure to thrive (due to nocturnal growth hormone suppression).

optionExplanations.A: Correct (this is the false statement). OSA-related daytime hypersomnolence increases, not decreases, the risk of motor vehicle collisions (by 2- to 7-fold).

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the pathophysiological consequences of obstructive sleep apnea, including fragmented REM sleep and increased accident risk.

questions.question: Which of the following does not cause hoarseness of voice?
questions.explanation: Hoarseness (dysphonia) results from impairment of vocal fold vibration or mobility. All intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid are innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN); the cricothyroid is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (SLN). In contrast, the INTERNAL branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is purely SENSORY to the supraglottic laryngeal mucosa (above the true vocal cords); its injury causes loss of the protective cough reflex and aspiration, but does NOT cause motor paralysis or hoarseness. High-yield pearl: Laryngeal Nerves: Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve = Motor to all intrinsic muscles except cricothyroid; injury -> vocal cord paralysis and HOARSENESS. Superior Laryngeal Nerve (Internal branch) = SENSORY above cords; injury -> aspiration, NO hoarseness. SLN (External branch) = Motor to cricothyroid; injury -> loss of high pitch. Exam trap: Isolated internal branch of SLN injury causes aspiration, NOT hoarseness. RLN injury causes hoarseness, NOT loss of supraglottic sensation.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is purely sensory above the cords; its injury causes aspiration, not hoarseness.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize that injury to the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve affects supraglottic sensation without causing hoarseness.

questions.question: All are absolute indications for tonsillectomy except:
questions.explanation: Indications for tonsillectomy are strictly stratified: ABSOLUTE indications include: 1) Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) with cor pulmonale, growth failure, or severe daytime somnolence; 2) Suspected malignant neoplasm (e.g., asymmetric tonsillar hypertrophy); and 3) Uncontrolled or recurrent hemorrhagic tonsillitis. In contrast, peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is a RELATIVE indication (often managed with needle aspiration/incision and drainage, reserving 'quinsy tonsillectomy' for recurrent abscess or children unable to tolerate drainage). High-yield pearl: Tonsillectomy Indications: Absolute: Severe OSA, Asymmetric tonsil (suspected malignancy), Uncontrolled hemorrhage. Relative: Recurrent bacterial tonsillitis (Paradise criteria: 7 episodes in 1 yr, 5/yr for 2 yrs, 3/yr for 3 yrs), Peritonsillar abscess. Exam trap: A single episode of peritonsillar abscess is NOT an absolute indication for immediate tonsillectomy; needle aspiration plus antibiotics is initial standard of care.

optionExplanations.A: Obstructive sleep apnea is an absolute indication for tonsillectomy.
optionExplanations.B: Hemorrhagic tonsillitis with life-threatening bleeding is an absolute indication.
optionExplanations.C: Suspected tonsillar malignancy (e.g., lymphoma, HPV-related SCC) is an absolute indication for diagnostic excision.
optionExplanations.D: Correct (the exception). Peritonsillar abscess is a relative, not absolute, indication; needle aspiration or incision and drainage is the initial treatment.

questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate absolute indications for tonsillectomy (OSA, suspected malignancy, severe hemorrhage) from relative indications.

questions.question: All of the following supply the lower pole of the palatine tonsils except:

options.B: Tonsillar branch of the facial artery

questions.explanation: The arterial supply of the palatine tonsil is derived from branches of the external carotid artery. The LOWER pole receives its blood supply from: 1) The tonsillar branch of the facial artery (the main and largest arterial feeder); 2) The dorsal lingual branches of the lingual artery; and 3) The ascending pharyngeal artery. In contrast, the ascending palatine artery (and lesser palatine artery) primarily enters and supplies the UPPER pole and soft palate. High-yield pearl: Tonsil Arterial Supply: Lower Pole: Tonsillar branch of Facial artery (main vessel), Ascending pharyngeal, Dorsal lingual. Upper Pole: Ascending palatine, Lesser palatine. Exam trap: Post-tonsillectomy primary hemorrhage most commonly originates from the tonsillar branch of the facial artery at the lower pole. [Source note - suspected source error: by the commonly cited assignment (lower pole = tonsillar branch of the facial, ascending palatine and dorsal lingual arteries; upper pole = ascending pharyngeal and lesser palatine arteries) the exception would be the ascending pharyngeal artery (option C), not option D. The source key (D) follows the source's own assignment and is retained; please verify against your course text.]

optionExplanations.A: Dorsal lingual artery supplies the anteroinferior pole of the tonsil.
optionExplanations.B: Tonsillar branch of the facial artery is the primary arterial supply entering the lower pole.
optionExplanations.C: Ascending pharyngeal artery enters the posteroinferior tonsil pole.
optionExplanations.D: Correct (the exception, per the source). The source assigns the ascending palatine artery to the upper pole and soft palate rather than the lower pole.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the arterial branches supplying the lower pole of the palatine tonsil.

questions.question: Which of the following is false regarding adenoid anatomy?

options.A: Receives minor branches from the internal maxillary artery
options.B: Receives minor branches from the facial artery
options.C: Formed during the 3rd-7th months of embryogenesis
options.D: Sensation is carried by CN IX and X
options.E: Receives blood supply from pharyngeal branches of the internal carotid artery

questions.explanation: Statement E is FALSE regarding adenoid (pharyngeal tonsil) anatomy because the adenoid receives its arterial blood supply entirely from branches of the EXTERNAL carotid artery (specifically the ascending pharyngeal artery, ascending palatine artery, pharyngeal branch of the maxillary artery, and tonsillar branch of the facial artery). The internal carotid artery gives NO branches in the neck or pharynx. High-yield pearl: Adenoid Anatomy: Located on the posterior wall of the nasopharynx. Arterial supply is exclusively from the EXTERNAL carotid artery branches (Ascending pharyngeal, Maxillary, Facial). Internal carotid artery gives NO branches in the neck. Exam trap: An aberrantly tortuous internal carotid artery may lie immediately deep to the posterior pharyngeal wall in rare cases, presenting an extreme surgical bleeding hazard during adenoidectomy.

optionExplanations.A: True: Receives minor pharyngeal branches from the internal maxillary artery (via the pterygopalatine canal).
optionExplanations.B: True: Receives branches from the ascending palatine branch of the facial artery.
optionExplanations.C: True: Formed during the 3rd to 7th months of fetal development.
optionExplanations.D: True: Sensory innervation of the nasopharynx is carried by CN IX and CN X.
optionExplanations.E: Correct (this is the false statement). The adenoid is supplied by external carotid branches; the internal carotid artery gives no branches in the neck.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall that the adenoid is vascularized by external carotid branches and receives no direct branches from the internal carotid artery.

questions.question: All are considered relative indications for tonsillectomy except:

options.A: Chronic tonsillitis refractory to antimicrobial therapy
options.D: Tonsillolithiasis with associated halitosis and pain

questions.explanation: Relative indications for tonsillectomy include: recurrent acute tonsillitis, chronic refractory tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess, dysphagia/speech distortion from tonsillar hypertrophy, and halitosis from tonsillolithiasis. Febrile seizures triggered by tonsillitis in children are also an accepted indication in many protocols. In this recall question, choice E is the designated answer. High-yield pearl: Paradise Criteria for Tonsillectomy in Recurrent Sore Throats: ≥ 7 episodes in the past year, OR ≥ 5 episodes/year for 2 years, OR ≥ 3 episodes/year for 3 years. Exam trap: Differentiate obstructive indications (sleep apnea, dysphagia) from infectious indications (Paradise criteria). [Source note - uncertain key: the source itself calls option E 'the designated answer' and states that tonsillitis-triggered febrile seizures are an accepted indication in many protocols.]

optionExplanations.A: Chronic tonsillitis refractory to medical therapy is a standard relative indication.
optionExplanations.B: Peritonsillar abscess is a recognized relative indication (quinsy tonsillectomy).
optionExplanations.C: Severe dysphagia due to tonsillar hypertrophy is an indication.
optionExplanations.D: Severe halitosis from recurrent tonsilloliths is a valid indication.
optionExplanations.E: Marked correct by the source as the 'designated answer'; the source also notes that tonsillitis-triggered febrile seizures are an accepted indication in many protocols.

questions.educationalObjective: Understand the clinical indications for tonsillectomy.

questions.question: Which of the following is considered a late complication of adenoid surgery?
questions.explanation: A recognized late complication of adenoidectomy is scarring and cicatricial stenosis of the Eustachian tube orifice (salpingopharyngeal fold), leading to chronic Eustachian tube dysfunction, persistent middle ear effusion, and conductive hearing loss. Other late complications include velopharyngeal insufficiency (hypernasal speech) and nasopharyngeal stenosis. High-yield pearl: Adenoidectomy Complications: Immediate: Primary hemorrhage, uvular injury. Reactionary: Bleeding within 24 hr. Late: Eustachian tube stenosis, Velopharyngeal insufficiency (hypernasality), Nasopharyngeal cicatricial stenosis, Grisel's syndrome. Exam trap: Always inspect the palate for submucous cleft palate (bifid uvula, zona pellucida, notch in hard palate) prior to adenoidectomy; removing adenoids unmasks severe velopharyngeal insufficiency. [Source note: option E reads 'atlanto-occipital' whereas the source's analysis and pearl discuss atlanto-axial subluxation (Grisel's syndrome); the key (D) is unaffected.]

optionExplanations.A: Soft palate damage is an immediate intraoperative mechanical complication.
optionExplanations.B: Dislocation of the cervical spine is an immediate intraoperative positioning complication.
optionExplanations.C: Reactionary hemorrhage occurs within the first 24 hours postoperatively.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Cicatricial stenosis of the Eustachian tube orifice is a recognized late complication of adenoidectomy.
optionExplanations.E: Atlanto-axial subluxation (Grisel's syndrome) is a rare post-infectious complication presenting within 1–2 weeks.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify Eustachian tube stenosis as a potential late cicatricial complication of adenoidectomy.

questions.question: Regarding recurrent respiratory papillomatosis, all are true except:

options.A: The most common site of the aerodigestive system affected is the larynx
options.B: The most common benign tumor of the larynx in children
options.C: The second most common cause of hoarseness in children after singer's nodules
options.D: Can be transmitted through orogenital sex or fetomaternally during delivery
options.E: The most common causative microorganisms are HPV 16 and 18

questions.explanation: Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis (RRP) is caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) types 6 and 11 (low-risk HPV types). Statement E claiming that HPV 16 and 18 are the causative organisms is FALSE. HPV 16 and 18 are high-risk oncogenic types that cause squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix and oropharynx. RRP is the most common benign laryngeal neoplasm in children, presenting with progressive hoarseness and stridor. High-yield pearl: Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis (RRP): Caused by HPV 6 and 11. Most common benign laryngeal tumor in children. Triad of presentation: Progressive hoarseness + Stridor + Respiratory distress. Histology: Squamous papillomas with fibrovascular cores. Exam trap: HPV 6 & 11 cause benign papillomatosis; HPV 16 & 18 cause malignant squamous cell carcinoma.

optionExplanations.A: True: The larynx (especially true and false vocal cords) is the most common site affected in the aerodigestive tract.
optionExplanations.B: True: RRP is the most common benign laryngeal tumor in the pediatric population.
optionExplanations.C: True: It is the second most common cause of childhood hoarseness after vocal nodules.
optionExplanations.D: True: Transmitted vertically from mother to neonate during passage through an infected birth canal.
optionExplanations.E: Correct (this is the false statement). RRP is caused by HPV types 6 and 11, not HPV 16 and 18.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify HPV 6 and 11 as the causative viruses of recurrent respiratory papillomatosis and distinguish them from high-risk oncogenic types.

questions.question: Which microorganism can present as a grey membrane (difficult to remove) on the tonsil surface?
questions.explanation: Corynebacterium diphtheriae produces a potent exotoxin (AB toxin that ADP-ribosylates elongation factor EF-2, halting protein synthesis). It produces a characteristic dense, tough, coalescent gray-green pseudomembrane firmly adherent to the tonsils and pharynx. Attempting to dislodge or scrape the membrane tears underlying submucosal capillaries, causing marked bleeding. Systemic toxin absorption causes myocarditis and polyneuropathy. High-yield pearl: Diphtheria: Caused by Corynebacterium diphtheriae. Hallmark: Adherent gray pseudomembrane that bleeds on scraping + Cervical lymphadenopathy ('bull neck'). Toxin inhibits EF-2. Treatment: Diphtheria antitoxin + Penicillin/Erythromycin. Exam trap: Never scrape or forcefully peel a suspected diphtheritic pseudomembrane; bleeding and catastrophic airway occlusion can occur.

optionExplanations.A: S. aureus produces purulent golden exudates, not an adherent gray pseudomembrane.
optionExplanations.B: EBV produces white-to-gray tonsillar exudates that wipe away easily without mucosal bleeding.
optionExplanations.C: H. influenzae causes epiglottitis and cellulitis.
optionExplanations.D: S. pneumoniae causes follicular tonsillar exudates.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Corynebacterium diphtheriae forms a dense, adherent gray pseudomembrane that bleeds when scraped.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify Corynebacterium diphtheriae as the organism producing an adherent gray pseudomembrane on the tonsils that bleeds upon removal.

questions.question: All of the following are indications for adenoidectomy except:

options.E: Neuromuscular abnormalities with impaired palatal function

questions.explanation: Adenoidectomy is indicated for adenoid hypertrophy causing obligate mouth breathing, obstructive sleep apnea, recurrent/chronic otitis media with effusion, and craniofacial maldevelopment (adenoid facies). In contrast, neuromuscular abnormalities with impaired palatal function (e.g., myasthenia gravis, cerebral palsy) and cleft palate / submucous cleft palate are strong CONTRAINDICATIONS to adenoidectomy, because the adenoid pad serves as a critical closure point for the defective palate; removing it causes severe, irreversible velopharyngeal insufficiency (hypernasality and nasal regurgitation). High-yield pearl: Adenoidectomy Contraindications: Submucous cleft palate (bifid uvula, hard palate notch), overt cleft palate, and neuromuscular palatal dysfunction. Excision causes severe velopharyngeal insufficiency. Exam trap: Always palpate the posterior border of the hard palate and inspect the uvula before adenoidectomy to rule out an occult submucous cleft.

optionExplanations.A: Chronic OME is an established indication for adenoidectomy.
optionExplanations.B: Obligate mouth breathing from nasopharyngeal obstruction is a classic indication.
optionExplanations.C: Recurrent OME in children undergoing second set of grommets is an indication.
optionExplanations.D: Severe orofacial abnormalities secondary to chronic adenoid facies benefit from adenoidectomy.
optionExplanations.E: Correct (the exception). Neuromuscular palatal dysfunction (and cleft palate) is a contraindication to adenoidectomy because removal causes severe velopharyngeal insufficiency.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize neuromuscular disorders with impaired palatal function as a contraindication to adenoidectomy.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT considered an absolute or relative contraindication for tonsillectomy?
questions.explanation: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is an ABSOLUTE INDICATION for tonsillectomy (and adenoidectomy), NOT a contraindication. Contraindications include bleeding disorders (hemophilia, von Willebrand disease), uncorrected severe anemia, acute systemic/respiratory infection, and uncontrolled severe cardiac or anesthetic risks. High-yield pearl: Adenotonsillectomy is the first-line curative surgical therapy for pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea. Exam trap: OSA is the most common indication for adenotonsillectomy in children today; never mistake an indication for a contraindication.

optionExplanations.A: Bleeding disorders are a major contraindication until coagulation factors are corrected.
optionExplanations.B: Severe cardiac conditions represent high anesthetic risks.
optionExplanations.C: Acute active infection increases bleeding risk and tissue friability.
optionExplanations.D: Severe anemia must be corrected before elective surgery.
optionExplanations.E: Correct (the exception). OSA is an indication for tonsillectomy, not a contraindication.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify obstructive sleep apnea as an absolute indication for tonsillectomy rather than a contraindication.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of secondary bleeding after tonsillectomy?
questions.explanation: Secondary post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage occurs more than 24 hours after surgery (most commonly between postoperative days 5 and 10). It is caused by premature separation or sloughing of the fibrinous tonsillar pseudomembrane (eschar) from the underlying healing muscle bed, almost invariably precipitated or exacerbated by local infection or severe dehydration. Primary hemorrhage occurs within the first 24 hours and is related to surgical technique. High-yield pearl: Post-Tonsillectomy Bleeding: Primary (< 24 hr): Due to surgical technique or slipped ligature. Secondary (> 24 hr, peak day 5–10): Due to premature sloughing of eschar, often triggered by local INFECTION. Exam trap: Any secondary post-tonsillectomy bleed—even a small 'herald bleed' that stopped—mandates immediate hospital observation and evaluation in the operating room.

optionExplanations.A: Aspirin causes primary intraoperative or early postoperative platelet dysfunction.
optionExplanations.B: Hemophilia causes early primary bleeding during or immediately following surgery.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Infection leading to premature sloughing of the eschar is the usual cause of secondary hemorrhage (peak days 5-10).

questions.educationalObjective: Identify infection as the primary predisposing factor for secondary post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage.

High-yield pearl: Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Repetitive pharyngeal collapse -> intermittent hypoxia -> systemic hypertension, pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale, polycythemia. In children: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is the #1 cause (cured by adenotonsillectomy). Exam trap: In children with OSA, sleepiness may manifest paradoxically as hyperactivity, behavioral problems, and failure to thrive (due to nocturnal growth hormone suppression).

optionExplanations.A: [Added] True statement, so not the answer: nocturnal growth hormone secretion is suppressed in children with OSA (source trap note).
optionExplanations.B: [Added] True statement, so not the answer: failure to thrive occurs in children with OSA.
optionExplanations.C: [Added] True statement, so not the answer: repetitive airway collapse causes intermittent hypoxemia and hypercapnia.

questions.question: Which condition can be detected by the Paul-Bunnell test?
questions.explanation: The Paul-Bunnell test (and the rapid Monospot test) detects heterophile IgM antibodies that agglutinate sheep (or horse) red blood cells, which is diagnostic for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infectious mononucleosis. These antibodies typically appear during the second to third week of illness and disappear within 4 to 6 months. High-yield pearl: Monospot / Paul-Bunnell Test: Detects heterophile antibodies for EBV. Can be falsely negative in the first week of illness and in young children < 4 years old (in whom EBV-specific VCA-IgM is preferred). Exam trap: Heterophile antibody tests have a ~25% false-negative rate in the first week of illness; repeat testing or EBV-specific serology is indicated if clinical suspicion remains high.

optionExplanations.A: Tuberculosis is diagnosed by PPD/interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA) and acid-fast bacilli smear/culture.
optionExplanations.B: S. aureus is identified by bacterial gram stain and culture.
optionExplanations.C: Diphtheria is diagnosed by Elek immunodiffusion toxigenicity testing and Loeffler/Tellurite culture.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The Paul-Bunnell/Monospot test detects heterophile IgM antibodies of EBV infectious mononucleosis.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the Paul-Bunnell test as a diagnostic tool for detecting heterophile antibodies in infectious mononucleosis.

questions.question: All of the following are manifestations of infectious mononucleosis except:
questions.explanation: Infectious mononucleosis characteristically produces reactive atypical CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytosis (>10% atypical lymphocytes on peripheral smear), absolute lymphocytosis, elevated hepatic transaminases, and mild hemolytic anemia or mild thrombocytopenia. In contrast, generalized PANCYTOPENIA (suppression of all three cell lines) is NOT a typical manifestation of uncomplicated mononucleosis; its appearance raises concern for aplastic anemia or hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). High-yield pearl: Mononucleosis Hematology: Atypical lymphocytosis (Downey cells, reactive CD8+ T cells reacting against infected B cells). Pancytopenia is abnormal. Exam trap: Atypical lymphocytes seen in infectious mononucleosis are reactive CD8+ T cells, NOT infected B cells (EBV infects B cells via CD21).

optionExplanations.A: Hepatomegaly occurs in ~10–15% of cases (with elevated transaminases in >80%).

questions.question: At which vertebral level is the cricoid cartilage located?
questions.explanation: The cricoid cartilage is the only complete ring-like cartilage in the respiratory tract. In the adult, the cricoid cartilage is located precisely at the level of the sixth cervical vertebra (C6). This level marks several critical anatomical transitions: 1) Junction of larynx with trachea, 2) Junction of pharynx with esophagus, 3) Level where the recurrent laryngeal nerve enters the larynx, and 4) Level of the carotid tubercle (Chassaignac's tubercle) where the common carotid artery can be compressed against C6. High-yield pearl: Anatomical Landmarks at C6: Cricoid cartilage, Laryngotracheal junction, Pharyngoesophageal junction, Middle cervical sympathetic ganglion, Carotid tubercle. Exam trap: In infants, the cricoid lies higher at C3–C4, descending to the adult C6 level by puberty.

optionExplanations.B: C5 corresponds to the mid-body of the thyroid cartilage.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The adult cricoid cartilage lies at the level of C6.
optionExplanations.D: T1 is located at the superior thoracic aperture, well below the larynx.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the C6 vertebral level as the anatomical location of the cricoid cartilage.

questions.question: All of the following statements about laryngomalacia are true EXCEPT:

options.A: It typically presents with inspiratory stridor starting around 4-6 weeks of age
options.B: Stridor worsens when the infant is supine and improves when prone or during crying
options.C: It is the most common cause of congenital stridor
options.D: Around 50% of cases require surgical intervention

questions.explanation: Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of congenital stridor in neonates and infants (~60–70% of cases). It is caused by delayed maturation of supporting laryngeal cartilages resulting in supraglottic collapse (inward collapse of floppy arytenoids and omega-shaped epiglottis) during inspiration. It presents with high-pitched inspiratory stridor starting around 4 to 6 weeks of life that worsens when supine or crying and improves when prone. Statement D is FALSE because around 90% of cases are mild/self-limiting and resolve spontaneously by 18 to 24 months; only 10% (NOT 50%) require surgical intervention (supraglottoplasty) for severe airway obstruction, apnea, or failure to thrive. High-yield pearl: Laryngomalacia: Most common congenital laryngeal anomaly. Inspiratory stridor worsening supine and during agitation, improving prone. Laryngoscopy: Tall 'omega-shaped' epiglottis with shortened aryepiglottic folds. Management: 90% conservative observation; 10% supraglottoplasty. questions.question: Which of the following statements about vocal cord nodules vs. polyps is incorrect?

options.A: Vocal cord nodules typically occur at the junction between the posterior 1/3 and anterior 2/3 of the membranous (vibratory) portion of the vocal folds
options.B: Vocal cord nodules are usually bilateral lesions and are more common in females
options.C: Vocal cord polyps are typically unilateral and may be associated with acute vocal trauma
options.D: Vocal cord polyps are often pedunculated and may be hemorrhagic
options.E: Polyps are more common in males and larger in size

questions.explanation: Statement A is INCORRECT because vocal cord nodules typically occur at the junction of the ANTERIOR 1/3 and POSTERIOR 2/3 of the true vocal cord (which represents the midpoint of the membranous, vibratory vocal fold where mechanical impact stress and aerodynamic collision forces are maximal). Nodules are typically bilateral and symmetric ('screamer's/singer's nodules') in young women or vocal abusers. In contrast, vocal cord polyps are characteristically unilateral, larger, pedunculated or sessile, and may be hemorrhagic, often following an acute episode of vocal trauma. High-yield pearl: Vocal Nodules vs Polyps: Nodules = Bilateral, symmetric, junction of anterior 1/3 and posterior 2/3. Treatment: Speech therapy first! Polyps = Unilateral, hemorrhagic/gelatinous, larger. Treatment: Surgical micro-laryngoscopy excision. Exam trap: First-line therapy for vocal nodules is ALWAYS speech therapy / voice rest; surgery is reserved only for mature fibrotic nodules unresponsive to therapy.

optionExplanations.A: Correct (this is the incorrect statement). Nodules lie at the junction of the anterior 1/3 and posterior 2/3 of the vocal fold, not the posterior 1/3 and anterior 2/3.
optionExplanations.B: True: Nodules are bilateral, symmetric lesions occurring in young females and professional voice users.
optionExplanations.C: True: Polyps are typically unilateral and frequently triggered by an acute shouting or vocal trauma incident.
optionExplanations.D: True: Polyps are often pedunculated with a distinct vascular/hemorrhagic component.
optionExplanations.E: True: Polyps have a male predominance and achieve larger dimensions than nodules.

questions.educationalObjective: Differentiate the anatomical location, symmetry, and pathology of vocal cord nodules versus polyps.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the innervation of the larynx is incorrect?

options.A: Recurrent laryngeal nerve innervates all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except cricothyroid
options.B: Superior laryngeal nerve's external branch supplies the cricothyroid muscle
options.C: Superior laryngeal nerve's internal branch supplies sensation to the supraglottic larynx
options.D: Recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies sensation to the infraglottic region
options.E: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the supraglottic larynx

questions.explanation: Statement E is INCORRECT because sensory innervation to the supraglottic larynx (above the vocal cords) is supplied by the INTERNAL branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (CN X). The EXTERNAL branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is purely MOTOR to the cricothyroid muscle (which tenses and elongates vocal folds to raise pitch). All other intrinsic laryngeal muscles and infraglottic sensation are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. High-yield pearl: Laryngeal Innervation Summary: All intrinsic muscles = RLN, EXCEPT Cricothyroid = External SLN. Sensation ABOVE vocal cords = Internal SLN; Sensation BELOW vocal cords = RLN. Exam trap: The external branch of the SLN courses adjacent to the superior thyroid artery; it can be inadvertently injured during thyroidectomy, causing loss of high-pitched voice.

optionExplanations.B: True: The external branch of the SLN innervates the cricothyroid muscle.
optionExplanations.C: True: The internal branch of the SLN provides sensory supply to the supraglottic mucosa.
optionExplanations.D: True: The recurrent laryngeal nerve provides sensation to the subglottis and upper trachea.
optionExplanations.E: Correct (this is the incorrect statement). The external branch of the SLN is purely motor to the cricothyroid; supraglottic sensation is carried by the internal branch.

questions.question: The vascular supply to a juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is primarily derived from which of the following arteries?
questions.explanation: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (JNA) is a benign, locally aggressive, highly vascular tumor of adolescent males. It originates in the posterolateral nasal wall near the sphenopalatine foramen. Its primary arterial blood supply is derived from the sphenopalatine artery and internal maxillary artery (from the external carotid artery system). Angiography with pre-operative embolization is standard of care to minimize catastrophic intraoperative hemorrhage. High-yield pearl: Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA): Adolescent male + Recurrent severe unprovoked epistaxis + Nasal obstruction. Primary blood supply = Internal Maxillary / Sphenopalatine Artery. BIOPSY IS CONTRAINDICATED in the clinic due to fatal hemorrhage risk! Perform pre-op embolization. Exam trap: NEVER biopsy a suspected JNA in an outpatient setting; massive life-threatening hemorrhage will occur.

optionExplanations.B: Ascending pharyngeal artery provides secondary collateral feeders to the skull base, but the primary feeder is the sphenopalatine / maxillary artery.
optionExplanations.C: Anterior ethmoidal artery (from ICA) may contribute collaterals if intracranial extension occurs, but is not the primary vessel.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The sphenopalatine/internal maxillary artery is the primary arterial supply of JNA.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the sphenopalatine artery as the primary vascular supply of juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma.

questions.question: All are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve except:
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) innervates all intrinsic muscles of the larynx (posterior cricoarytenoid, lateral cricoarytenoid, transverse and oblique arytenoids, and thyroarytenoid/vocalis) EXCEPT the cricothyroid muscle, which is innervated by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. questions.question: A man with aphonia and an immobile unilateral vocal cord should undergo:

options.A: CT of the neck and chest

questions.question: Initial step in a patient with drooling, high-grade fever, and other symptoms:
questions.explanation: Acute epiglottitis (supraglottitis) is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening airway infection characterized by high fever (≥39°C), severe odynophagia, drooling of saliva, inspiratory stridor, toxic appearance, and a muffled 'hot potato' voice. questions.question: Reinke's edema is best visualized by:
questions.explanation: Reinke's edema is diffuse, bilateral polypoid degeneration of the superficial lamina propria (Reinke's space) of the vocal folds. It is strongly linked to chronic cigarette smoking and chronic voice abuse, presenting with a characteristically low-pitched, coarse, gravelly voice (often striking in middle-aged female smokers). It is best visualized by flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy (showing floppy, water-bag translucent swelling along the entire cord). Statement claiming decreasing smoking does not improve prognosis is FALSE; strict smoking cessation is the essential foundation of management that halts progression and can reverse early edema. Voice: Abnormally deep, gravelly voice. Management: Smoking cessation first; micro-laryngoscopic suctioning if airway is compromised. Exam trap: Do not perform surgery on Reinke's edema without smoking cessation; continuing to smoke postoperatively causes rapid recurrence and vocal fold scarring.

questions.question: Presbylaryngis is:
questions.explanation: Presbylaryngis refers to the physiological, age-related changes in the voice and laryngeal architecture. questions.question: Waldeyer's ring involves lymphoid tissues in:
questions.explanation: Waldeyer's lymphatic ring is an annular ring of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) encircling the entrance to the aerodigestive tract. questions.question: The nerve supply of the piriformis fossa is:

questions.question: The most common laryngeal cancer is:
questions.explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) accounts for greater than 95% of all primary malignant neoplasms of the larynx. It is overwhelmingly associated with chronic tobacco smoking and excessive alcohol consumption, which act synergistically. questions.question: A teacher with hoarseness of voice for two months. Treatment is:
questions.explanation: A teacher presenting with hoarseness of voice for two months due to vocal cord nodules (singer's/screamer's nodules) should be managed primarily with speech and voice therapy. Vocal nodules are inflammatory calluses in the superficial lamina propria resulting from mechanical vocal abuse and hyperfunctional phonation. Behavioral voice therapy improves vocal hygiene, teaches resonant voice production, and resolves nodules in over 85–90% of cases. Surgical excision is contraindicated initially as it carries risk of vocal fold scarring. High-yield pearl: Vocal Cord Nodules Treatment: First-line = Voice / Speech Therapy and vocal hygiene. Surgery is strictly contraindicated unless nodules fail prolonged comprehensive therapy. Exam trap: Do NOT operate on vocal nodules without attempting voice therapy; scarring of the lamina propria causes permanent, irreversible dysphonia.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Voice/speech therapy with vocal hygiene is first-line for vocal cord nodules; early surgery risks vocal fold scarring.

questions.educationalObjective: Recommend speech and voice therapy as the definitive first-line management for vocal cord nodules.

questions.question: In unilateral vocal cord paralysis, what should be done?
questions.explanation: In patients with acute unilateral vocal cord paralysis (idiopathic or post-viral neuropraxia), initial management consists of observation and speech therapy with follow-up over 6 to 12 months. Spontaneous recovery of nerve function occurs in a substantial proportion of patients during this period. Permanent medialization thyroplasty (Isshiki Type I) is reserved for patients whose nerve function fails to recover after 12 months. High-yield pearl: Unilateral Vocal Cord Paralysis: If imaging is clear, observe for 6–12 months to allow for spontaneous axonal reinnervation. Temporary injection laryngoplasty can provide interim symptomatic relief. Exam trap: Do not perform permanent medialization surgery (type 1 thyroplasty) before 6–12 months have elapsed.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Once imaging is clear, observe with speech therapy for 6-12 months before permanent medialization.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify observation for 6 to 12 months as the initial management strategy for unilateral vocal cord paralysis.

questions.question: Voice production depends on all of the following except:
questions.explanation: According to the myoelastic-aerodynamic theory of phonation, voice production requires: 1) Vocal cord adduction (bringing cords into the midline airstream), 2) Subglottic air pressure generation, 3) Intact recurrent laryngeal nerve innervation to maintain muscle tone and positioning, and 4) Transglottic air flow to trigger Bernoulli aerodynamic mucosal wave vibration. Vocal cord elongation adjusts acoustic pitch and fundamental frequency, but is NOT an absolute requirement for primary voice production. High-yield pearl: Phonation Requirements: Vocal cord adduction + Subglottic air pressure + Intact nerve supply + Airflow. Vocal cord elongation (by cricothyroid) alters pitch, not the generation of sound. Exam trap: Paralysis of adduction results in a breathy, aphonic voice due to air escape.

optionExplanations.A: Intact nerve supply is necessary to adduct and position the vocal cords.
optionExplanations.B: Correct (the exception). Vocal cord elongation adjusts pitch but is not required to generate voice.
optionExplanations.C: Vocal cord adduction is essential to create a subglottic pressure seal for phonation.
optionExplanations.D: Airflow from the lungs provides the driving energy for mucosal wave vibration.
optionExplanations.E: Subglottic pressure buildup is mandatory to separate the cords and initiate phonation.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the physiological requirements for voice production and recognize that vocal cord elongation alters pitch rather than generating phonation.

questions.question: The only abductor muscle of the vocal cords is:
questions.explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid (PCA) muscle is the ONLY abductor of the vocal cords. It originates on the posterior surface of the cricoid lamina and inserts into the muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage. When it contracts, it rotates the arytenoids outward and pulls the vocal processes apart, opening the rima glottidis for respiration. Bilateral paralysis of the PCA (as in bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury) leaves the cords in an adducted paramedian position, causing acute stridor and asphyxiation requiring immediate tracheostomy. High-yield pearl: Laryngeal Muscles Rule: 'Posticus Pulls cords apart' -> Posterior Cricoarytenoid is the SOLE vocal cord abductor. Lateral cricoarytenoid and interarytenoids are adductors. Cricothyroid tenses cords (raises pitch). Exam trap: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury paralyzes the posterior cricoarytenoid muscles, leaving cords adducted -> catastrophic acute airway obstruction!

optionExplanations.A: Cricothyroid tenses and elongates the vocal cords to raise pitch.
optionExplanations.B: Lateral cricoarytenoid is a primary adductor of the vocal folds.
optionExplanations.C: Transverse arytenoid adducts the posterior cartilaginous glottis.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor of the vocal cords.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle as the sole abductor of the vocal cords.

questions.question: A 60-year-old male, heavy smoker, presents with worsening hoarseness of voice for 3 months. On laryngoscopy, a lesion on the left vocal cord is found. What should you do next?

options.C: CT of the neck and chest

questions.explanation: A 60-year-old male with a heavy smoking history presenting with progressive hoarseness of voice for 3 months and an identifiable vocal cord lesion has laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma until proven otherwise. Any patient with hoarseness lasting more than 2 to 3 weeks must undergo direct visual evaluation of the larynx. When a suspicious vocal cord lesion (leukoplakia, exophytic mass, or ulceration) is visualized, the mandatory next step is direct laryngoscopy and biopsy under general anesthesia to obtain histological tissue confirmation and stage the lesion. High-yield pearl: Hoarseness > 2–3 weeks in a smoker = Laryngeal Cancer until proven otherwise! Mandatory next step: Direct laryngoscopy and excisional/incisional biopsy. Exam trap: Never initiate empiric speech therapy or reflux treatment in an older smoker with persistent hoarseness without inspecting and biopsying the vocal cords.

optionExplanations.A: MRI provides soft tissue evaluation, but tissue biopsy is mandatory to confirm malignancy.
optionExplanations.B: PET scan is used for distant metastasis staging, not primary histological diagnosis.
optionExplanations.C: CT neck/chest is used for regional staging, but definitive histological diagnosis requires biopsy.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. A persistent suspicious vocal cord lesion in a smoker requires direct laryngoscopy with biopsy for tissue diagnosis.

questions.educationalObjective: Recommend direct laryngoscopy and biopsy for persistent hoarseness with an identified vocal cord mass in a smoker.

questions.question: Regarding the anatomy of the larynx, which statement is false?

options.B: Extrinsic muscles adjust the position of the larynx
options.C: Intrinsic muscles control the tension of the vocal cords
options.D: Consists of one bone and 8 cartilages

questions.explanation: Statement D is FALSE because the skeletal framework of the larynx consists of one bone (the hyoid bone) and NINE cartilages (3 unpaired and 3 paired): Unpaired = Thyroid, Cricoid, and Epiglottis (3 cartilages); Paired = Arytenoid, Corniculate, and Cuneiform (6 cartilages). Total = 9 cartilages, NOT 8. High-yield pearl: Laryngeal Cartilage Count = 9 total. Unpaired (3): Thyroid, Cricoid, Epiglottis. Paired (3 pairs = 6): Arytenoid, Corniculate, Cuneiform. Exam trap: The true vocal folds are covered by non-keratinizing stratified squamous epithelium to withstand mechanical collision, unlike the rest of the respiratory tract.

optionExplanations.A: True: The larynx is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar respiratory epithelium, except over the true vocal cords (which are lined by protective stratified squamous epithelium).
optionExplanations.B: True: Extrinsic laryngeal muscles (strap muscles, suprahyoid muscles) elevate and depress the larynx in the neck.
optionExplanations.C: True: Intrinsic laryngeal muscles adjust the tension, length, and position of the vocal folds.
optionExplanations.D: Correct (this is the false statement). The laryngeal skeleton has one bone (the hyoid) and nine cartilages, not eight.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall that the laryngeal skeleton consists of nine cartilages (three unpaired and three paired).

questions.question: All of the following can cause vocal cord palsy except:
questions.explanation: Vocal cord paralysis results from neurological disruption of the recurrent or superior laryngeal nerves, or mechanical fixation of the cricoarytenoid joint. Recognized causes include: iatrogenic surgical trauma (thyroidectomy, carotid endarterectomy, anterior cervical discectomy), bronchogenic carcinoma (apical/mediastinal compression), cricoarytenoid rheumatoid arthritis, myasthenia gravis, and sarcoidosis neuropathy. In contrast, croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) is an acute viral mucosal inflammation causing subglottic edema and barking cough; it does NOT cause neurogenic vocal cord paralysis. High-yield pearl: Vocal Cord Paralysis Causes: Surgical (thyroidectomy), Malignant (lung, esophageal, thyroid cancer), Neurological (stroke, ALS), Cricoarytenoid ankylosis (rheumatoid arthritis). Croup causes subglottic mucosal narrowing, not nerve palsy. Exam trap: If a patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis develops stridor, think cricoarytenoid joint fixation!

optionExplanations.A: Correct (the exception). Croup is an acute subglottic mucosal inflammation and does not cause nerve palsy.
optionExplanations.B: Thyroid surgery is a classic iatrogenic cause of recurrent laryngeal nerve injury.
optionExplanations.C: Bronchogenic carcinoma invading the recurrent laryngeal nerve is the leading malignant cause of vocal cord paralysis.
optionExplanations.D: Rheumatoid arthritis can cause cricoarytenoid joint ankylosis, mimicking vocal cord paralysis.
optionExplanations.E: Myasthenia gravis can produce flaccid vocal cord paresis due to neuromuscular junction acetylcholine receptor failure.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify etiologies of vocal cord palsy and recognize that viral croup does not cause nerve paralysis.

questions.question: The most common neoplastic cause of vocal cord paralysis is:
questions.explanation: The most common neoplastic cause of vocal cord paralysis is bronchial (bronchogenic) carcinoma of the lung. Because the left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops deep into the mediastinum beneath the aortic arch, it is extraordinarily vulnerable to direct invasion or compression by primary lung tumors (especially left upper lobe cancers) or subcarinal/aortopulmonary window lymphadenopathy. High-yield pearl: Most common malignant cause of left vocal cord palsy = Bronchogenic Carcinoma (Ortner's syndrome / cardiovocal syndrome if from left atrial enlargement). Exam trap: Any unexplained left vocal cord paralysis requires chest imaging (CT chest) to rule out an occult apical lung tumor.

optionExplanations.A: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma affects cranial nerves at the skull base (CN IX, X, XI, XII), but is less common overall than lung cancer.
optionExplanations.B: Laryngeal carcinoma causes cord fixation through direct muscle invasion, but bronchial carcinoma is the most common extrinsic cause.
optionExplanations.C: Thyroid carcinoma can invade the recurrent laryngeal nerve in the tracheoesophageal groove, but lung cancer is epidemiologically far more frequent.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Bronchogenic carcinoma is the most common neoplastic cause, especially via the left recurrent laryngeal nerve in the mediastinum.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify bronchogenic carcinoma as the leading neoplastic etiology of vocal cord paralysis.

questions.question: Which statement about recurrent respiratory papillomatosis is false?
questions.explanation: [Added] The source gave only a generic placeholder explanation for this question. questions.question: A 3-year-old boy presents to the emergency room with fever (39°C orally), odynophagia, drooling of saliva, respiratory distress, and muffled voice for 24 hours. Regarding this patient, all are true EXCEPT:

options.A: "Thumb" sign on neck X-ray is not necessary for diagnosis
options.B: Blood cultures are not always positive
options.C: He should be taken to the operating room for intubation and direct laryngoscopy
options.D: IV antibiotics have a major role in management
options.E: Throat examination by tongue depressor should be done as soon as possible

questions.explanation: Acute epiglottitis (supraglottitis) is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening airway infection characterized by high fever (≥39°C), severe odynophagia, drooling of saliva, inspiratory stridor, toxic appearance, and a muffled 'hot potato' voice. The immediate initial priority is to SECURE THE AIRWAY in a controlled setting (the operating room with ENT and anesthesia prepared for immediate rigid bronchoscopy or emergency tracheostomy). Direct examination of the pharynx with a tongue depressor is strictly CONTRAINDICATED because tactile stimulation of the pharynx can trigger fatal reflex laryngospasm and complete airway arrest. High-yield pearl: Acute Epiglottitis: High fever + Drooling + Tripod position + Muffled voice. Immediate action: SECURE AIRWAY in OR. DO NOT examine throat with a tongue depressor! Exam trap: Never use a tongue depressor or agitate a child with suspected epiglottitis; reflex laryngospasm can cause immediate fatal cardiac arrest.

optionExplanations.A: True: 'Thumb' sign on lateral neck X-ray is classic but not required and should never delay airway management.
optionExplanations.B: True: Blood cultures are positive in only ~70% of cases.
optionExplanations.C: True: Endotracheal intubation under direct visualization in the operating room is the gold standard.
optionExplanations.D: True: IV third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone) plus antistaphylococcal coverage is crucial.
optionExplanations.E: Correct (this is the false statement). Tongue-depressor examination is contraindicated in suspected epiglottitis because it can trigger fatal laryngospasm.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify airway stabilization as the emergency priority in epiglottitis and recognize that tongue depressor examination is contraindicated.

questions.question: A 40-year-old male presents to the ENT clinic with aphonia and hemoptysis. Fiberoptic laryngoscopy shows an immobile right vocal cord. The patient has no significant medical or surgical history. What is the next step?

options.E: CT of the neck and chest

questions.explanation: A patient presenting with aphonia/hoarseness and an immobile vocal cord on fiberoptic laryngoscopy requires an urgent CT scan of the neck and chest with intravenous contrast. This is because the recurrent laryngeal nerve follows an extensive course: the left RLN loops under the aortic arch in the mediastinum, and the right RLN loops around the right subclavian artery. Malignancies along this pathway (e.g., bronchogenic carcinoma, apical Pancoast tumor, mediastinal adenopathy, esophageal carcinoma, or thyroid malignancy) must be excluded before assuming an idiopathic etiology. High-yield pearl: Unexplained Vocal Cord Paralysis: CT of Neck and Chest from skull base to aortopulmonary window is mandatory to trace the entire course of the recurrent laryngeal nerves and rule out bronchogenic carcinoma. Exam trap: Left vocal cord paralysis is more common than right because the left RLN has a longer intrathoracic course under the aortic arch.

optionExplanations.A: Thyroplasty is a surgical medialization procedure performed only after definitive etiology is identified and 6–12 months have elapsed without spontaneous recovery.
optionExplanations.B: Observation is appropriate only AFTER malignant and structural causes have been definitively ruled out by cross-sectional imaging.
optionExplanations.C: Vocal cord injection is a therapeutic medialization intervention, not the initial diagnostic workup.
optionExplanations.D: Ultrasound of the neck assesses the thyroid, but fails to visualize the mediastinum and pulmonary parenchyma where lung tumors compress the left RLN.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. CT of the neck and chest is needed to exclude a malignant cause (e.g., bronchogenic or apical tumor) along the course of the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

questions.educationalObjective: Recommend contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and chest as the essential next step to evaluate unexplained unilateral vocal cord paralysis.

questions.question: What is the best indicator of the anatomic level of airway obstruction?

options.E: The respiratory phase during which stridor occurs

questions.explanation: The respiratory phase during which stridor occurs is the single best clinical indicator of the anatomical level of upper airway obstruction: 1) Inspiratory stridor indicates obstruction at or above the glottis (supraglottic/extrathoracic airway, e.g., laryngomalacia, epiglottitis, retropharyngeal abscess); 2) Biphasic stridor indicates fixed obstruction at the glottis or subglottis (e.g., subglottic stenosis, croup, bilateral cord palsy); and 3) Expiratory stridor/wheezing indicates intrathoracic tracheobronchial obstruction (e.g., tracheomalacia, bronchial foreign body). High-yield pearl: Stridor Timing & Anatomic Level: Inspiratory = Supraglottic (Laryngomalacia, Epiglottitis). Biphasic = Glottic / Subglottic (Subglottic stenosis, Croup). Expiratory = Tracheobronchial (Foreign body, Tracheomalacia). Exam trap: Inspiratory stridor worsens when airway collapses under negative inspiratory pressure; expiratory stridor occurs when intrathoracic airway collapses under positive pleural pressure.

optionExplanations.A: Respiratory rate reflects work of breathing and metabolic demand, but does not localize the anatomic level.
optionExplanations.B: Posturing (e.g., tripoding) indicates severe distress, not the precise level.
optionExplanations.C: Cyanosis reflects advanced hypoxemia, not the anatomical site.
optionExplanations.D: Eating difficulties indicate coordination issues, not the airway level.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The respiratory phase of stridor (inspiratory, biphasic or expiratory) is the best clinical indicator of the level of obstruction.

questions.educationalObjective: Use the respiratory phase of stridor (inspiratory, biphasic, or expiratory) to determine the anatomical level of airway obstruction.

questions.question: All of the following can cause vocal cord paralysis except:
questions.explanation: Vocal cord immobility can be caused by neurogenic paralysis (surgical trauma, cervical spine surgery, mediastinal/skull base tumors), granulomatous neuropathy (sarcoidosis, tuberculosis), or idiopathic neuritis. In contrast, uncomplicated acute laryngitis is a superficial mucosal inflammation of the vocal cords causing hoarseness, erythema, and edema; it does NOT cause neurogenic vocal cord paralysis. High-yield pearl: Laryngitis causes hoarseness due to mucosal edema, but vocal cord mobility on laryngoscopy remains completely intact. Exam trap: True vocal cord paralysis shows lack of vocal cord abduction/adduction; acute laryngitis shows full cord excursion despite mucosal edema.

optionExplanations.A: Iatrogenic injury is the leading cause of unilateral vocal cord paralysis.
optionExplanations.B: Sarcoidosis can cause cranial neuropathies affecting CN X and the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
optionExplanations.C: Idiopathic vocal cord paralysis accounts for ~20–25% of cases.
optionExplanations.D: Direct neck or thoracic trauma can transect or crush the laryngeal nerves.
optionExplanations.E: Correct (the exception). Acute laryngitis is mucosal inflammation with preserved cord mobility and does not cause paralysis.

questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish acute mucosal laryngitis from conditions that cause true neurogenic vocal cord paralysis.

questions.question: The most common presentation of supraglottic laryngeal cancer is:
questions.explanation: Unlike glottic cancers (which present early with persistent hoarseness due to impaired vocal cord vibration), supraglottic laryngeal cancers (arising on the epiglottis, false vocal cords, or aryepiglottic folds) often remain asymptomatic for long periods until presenting with cervical metastatic lymph nodes (Level II/III). This occurs because the supraglottic larynx possesses an exceptionally rich, bilateral submucosal lymphatic drainage network, resulting in cervical nodal metastases in 40–50% of patients at initial diagnosis. High-yield pearl: Laryngeal Cancer Presentation: Glottic (60%): Presents EARLY with HOARSENESS. Rare early metastasis. Excellent cure rate. Supraglottic (35%): Presents LATE with CERVICAL METASTASIS (40–50%), throat pain, referred otalgia, or globus sensation. Exam trap: Any adult presenting with an asymptomatic, firm neck mass (Level II/III) must undergo flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy to evaluate the supraglottis and oropharynx.

optionExplanations.A: Referred otalgia occurs via CN X, but palpable cervical nodal metastasis is the most common presenting sign.
optionExplanations.B: Shortness of breath occurs only in late bulky obstructive tumors.
optionExplanations.C: Hoarseness is the hallmark of glottic cancer, but appears late in supraglottic cancer when the true cords become invaded.
optionExplanations.D: Dysphagia is common, but cervical lymphadenopathy is the classic primary presentation.
optionExplanations.E: Correct per source key. The rich bilateral lymphatics of the supraglottis lead to cervical nodal metastases (40-50% at diagnosis), often the presenting sign.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify cervical metastatic lymphadenopathy as the most common initial presentation of supraglottic laryngeal cancer.

questions.question: The smallest segment of the facial nerve is:
questions.explanation: The facial nerve (CN VII) consists of intracranial, intratemporal, and extratemporal segments. The intratemporal course has four segments: 1) Meatal (in internal auditory canal, 8–10 mm), 2) Labyrinthine (3–4 mm), 3) Tympanic/horizontal (8–11 mm), and 4) Mastoid/vertical (13 mm). The LABYRINTHINE segment is both the SMALLEST (shortest, 3–4 mm) and NARROWEST (diameter ~0.68 mm) segment of the fallopian canal. Because of this rigid bony confinement and lack of epineurial connective tissue, any inflammatory edema of the facial nerve (as in Bell's palsy) causes immediate entrapment ischemia and conduction block at the labyrinthine segment. High-yield pearl: Facial Nerve Segments: Shortest and Narrowest = LABYRINTHINE segment (3–4 mm, 0.68 mm). Most vulnerable to entrapment in Bell's palsy! Longest intratemporal = Mastoid segment (13 mm). Exam trap: The labyrinthine segment is the narrowest point of the fallopian canal; entrapment edema here is the primary pathophysiological trigger of Bell's palsy.

optionExplanations.A: Tympanic segment is ~8–11 mm long, running above the oval window.
optionExplanations.B: Mastoid segment is the longest intratemporal segment (~13 mm), giving off the nerve to stapedius and chorda tympani.
optionExplanations.C: Cranial/intracranial segment is the root entry zone between brainstem and IAC (~23–24 mm).
optionExplanations.D: Meatal segment is ~8–10 mm long within the internal auditory meatus.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The labyrinthine segment (3-4 mm long, about 0.68 mm wide) is the shortest and narrowest segment.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the labyrinthine segment as the shortest and narrowest segment of the facial nerve.

questions.question: Which of the following is an indication for surgical intervention in a patient with facial nerve palsy?

options.A: Grade II facial nerve palsy due to Bell's palsy
options.B: Grade IV facial nerve palsy associated with middle ear cholesteatoma
options.C: Facial nerve palsy with vesicular rash on the external ear
options.D: Facial nerve palsy occurring 2 hours after parotid surgery with no improvement
options.E: Grade VI facial nerve palsy without symptoms

questions.explanation: Facial nerve paralysis developing in the setting of chronic suppurative otitis media or middle ear cholesteatoma is an ABSOLUTE INDICATION for emergency surgical intervention (tympanomastoidectomy and facial nerve decompression/exploration). Cholesteatoma causes osteolytic enzymatic bone erosion of the fallopian canal (most commonly the tympanic segment), causing direct nerve compression and bacterial neuritis. Emergency surgical removal of cholesteatoma is mandatory to halt permanent axonal death. High-yield pearl: Facial Nerve Palsy Surgical Indications: Traumatic immediate complete paralysis with temporal bone fracture; Cholesteatoma-associated paralysis; Malignant neoplasm. Bell's palsy and Ramsay Hunt are managed MEDICALLY! Exam trap: Facial palsy + Otitis Media / Cholesteatoma = Urgent surgery! Medical treatment alone will result in permanent facial disfigurement.

optionExplanations.A: Grade II Bell's palsy is mild paresis managed conservatively with oral corticosteroids (prednisone); surgery is contraindicated.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Facial palsy with cholesteatoma is an indication for urgent surgery (tympanomastoidectomy with nerve decompression).
optionExplanations.C: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (vesicular rash) is managed medically with high-dose oral corticosteroids and oral valacyclovir/acyclovir.
optionExplanations.D: Facial weakness 2 hours after parotidectomy is typically due to local anesthetic diffusion; observation is indicated unless the nerve was known to be transected intraoperatively.
optionExplanations.E: Complete paralysis without identifiable etiology requires diagnostic imaging, not unindicated blind surgery.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize middle ear cholesteatoma with facial nerve palsy as a clear indication for urgent surgical intervention.

questions.question: False about facial palsy:

options.A: CT to rule out infectious cause or neoplasm
options.B: Acute otitis media is the most common cause of Bell's palsy

questions.explanation: Statement B is FALSE because acute otitis media is NOT the most common cause of Bell's palsy. Bell's palsy is by definition an IDIOPATHIC acute peripheral lower motor neuron facial paralysis, strongly linked to reactivation of Herpes Simplex Virus Type 1 (HSV-1) within the geniculate ganglion. While acute otitis media can cause inflammatory facial palsy (via canal dehiscence), that is classified as otitis-induced facial palsy, not Bell's palsy. High-yield pearl: Bell's Palsy: Acute, unilateral, idiopathic lower motor neuron facial palsy. Peak onset < 72 hours. Pathophysiology: HSV-1 reactivation in geniculate ganglion causing labyrinthine segment edema. First-line therapy: Oral Prednisone (60 mg/day for 7–10 days) started within 72 hours. Exam trap: Forehead involvement differentiates peripheral LMN palsy (forehead affected, cannot wrinkle brow) from central UMN stroke (forehead spared due to bilateral cortical innervation).

optionExplanations.A: True: CT or MRI is indicated if atypical features, progression beyond 3 weeks, or non-recovery occurs, to rule out neoplasms (schwannoma, parotid tumor) or occult osteomyelitis.
optionExplanations.B: Correct (this is the false statement). Bell's palsy is idiopathic (HSV-1 reactivation), not caused by acute otitis media.

questions.educationalObjective: Recall that Bell's palsy is an idiopathic reactivation of HSV-1 rather than a complication of acute otitis media.

questions.question: Which of the following is false regarding facial nerve palsy?

options.A: Bell's palsy may involve decreased tearing or altered taste sensation
options.B: Radiologic tests are not indicated for the assessment of every patient presenting with facial nerve paralysis
options.C: CT is the test of choice for facial nerve paralysis secondary to inflammatory and neoplastic causes
options.D: Any palsy with progression should be considered a neoplasm until proven otherwise

questions.explanation: Statement C is FALSE because Contrast-Enhanced Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) with gadolinium—NOT CT—is the imaging modality of choice for evaluating facial nerve paralysis secondary to inflammatory, viral, and neoplastic etiologies. Gadolinium MRI provides superior soft tissue resolution of the brainstem, cerebellopontine angle, IAC, and fallopian canal, clearly demonstrating facial nerve schwannomas, perineural tumor spread, or intense contrast enhancement of the intratemporal nerve. CT is the test of choice for temporal bone fractures and bony erosion. High-yield pearl: Facial Palsy Imaging: Trauma / Fractures = High-Resolution CT. Tumor / Neoplasm / Inflammatory / Recurrent = Gadolinium MRI of brain/IAC. Exam trap: Progressive facial palsy over months is NEVER Bell's palsy; it is a tumor (facial neuroma, acoustic neuroma, parotid malignancy) until proven otherwise.

optionExplanations.A: True: Bell's palsy involves branches of CN VII, including chorda tympani (taste loss) and greater petrosal nerve (reduced lacrimation).
optionExplanations.B: True: Routine imaging is NOT recommended for typical acute Bell's palsy that improves within expected timelines.
optionExplanations.C: Correct (this is the false statement). Gadolinium MRI, not CT, is the imaging modality of choice for inflammatory and neoplastic causes.
optionExplanations.D: True: Any facial palsy that progresses insidiously over > 3 weeks or fails to recover after 3–4 months must be presumed neoplastic until proven otherwise.
optionExplanations.E: [Added] Incorrect, because statement C is false.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify MRI with contrast, rather than CT, as the optimal imaging test for inflammatory and neoplastic causes of facial nerve paralysis.

questions.question: The facial nerve supplies all of the following except:

questions.question: Which statement is true regarding axonotmesis (in facial nerve injury)?

options.A: Electrophysiologic studies yield evidence of complete nerve degeneration
options.B: Characterized by both Wallerian degeneration and loss of endoneural tubules
options.C: The nerve is viable and returns to normal function when the blockade is corrected
options.E: Electrically, the nerve shows rapid and complete degeneration, with loss of voluntary motor units

questions.explanation: Under the Seddon/Sunderland classification of nerve trauma: In Axonotmesis (Class II), the axon is disrupted, leading to Wallerian degeneration distal to the injury site. However, the supporting connective tissue sheaths (endoneurium, perineurium, epineurium) remain intact. Electrophysiologically, the nerve exhibits complete denervation changes (fibrillations and loss of voluntary motor unit action potentials) after 48–72 hours. Because the endoneurial tubes remain continuous, axons can regenerate at a rate of 1 mm/day with excellent functional recovery. High-yield pearl: Nerve Injury Classification: Neuropraxia (Class I): Physiological conduction block, intact axons, complete rapid recovery. Axonotmesis (Class II): Axonal transection + Wallerian degeneration, INTACT endoneurium, regenerates ~1 mm/day. Neurotmesis (Class III-V): Complete nerve transection, disruption of sheaths, requires surgical repair. Exam trap: Electroneurography (ENoG) must be performed between days 3 and 14 after injury; earlier testing reflects false normal distal viability. [Source note: option A (complete degeneration on electrophysiologic testing) overlaps with the key, option E; the source key (E) is retained.]

optionExplanations.A: Electrophysiologic studies show loss of conduction distal to the lesion after Wallerian degeneration (48–72 hours), but nerve tubes remain intact.
optionExplanations.B: Loss of endoneurial tubules occurs in neurotmesis (Sunderland IV/V), not axonotmesis.
optionExplanations.C: Immediate return of function upon blockade correction describes neuropraxia (Class I), not axonotmesis.
optionExplanations.D: Normal electrophysiologic conduction distal to the lesion after 72 hours is seen in neuropraxia.
optionExplanations.E: Correct per source key. In axonotmesis, electrophysiology shows complete degeneration with loss of voluntary motor units, while the endoneurial tubes stay intact.

questions.question: All of the following are true regarding Bell's palsy except:

optionExplanations.D: Correct (the exception). Bell's palsy is overwhelmingly sporadic; familial cases account for under about 4-8%.

questions.explanation: After exiting the stylomastoid foramen, the facial nerve enters the parotid gland and branches into five major terminal motor divisions: Temporal (frontal), Zygomatic, Buccal, Marginal Mandibular, and Cervical ('To Zanzibar By Motor Car'). questions.question: An 18-year-old Chinese patient presents with unilateral middle ear effusion and loud tinnitus. He has a history of recurrent tonsillitis. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: In an adult—particularly of southern Chinese, East Asian, or North African descent—presenting with new-onset unilateral middle ear effusion (glue ear), aural fullness, and loud tinnitus, nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) must be ruled out immediately. NPC characteristically arises from the fossa of Rosenmüller (posterolateral pharyngeal recess) and infiltrates the Eustachian tube. Strongly linked to Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV). Initial step: Flexible Nasopharyngoscopy. Exam trap: Never place a grommet in an adult with unilateral glue ear without first examining the nasopharynx to exclude NPC!

questions.question: Trotter's triad includes all of the following except:

SENSORINEURAL hearing loss is NOT part of Trotter's triad (the hearing loss is purely conductive). questions.question: What is the most common histological type of laryngeal cancer?
questions.explanation: Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is by far the most common histological type of head and neck cancer, accounting for >90–95% of all malignant neoplasms of the oral cavity, pharynx, and larynx. It arises from the mucosal stratified squamous epithelium, strongly associated with tobacco use, alcohol abuse, and high-risk oncogenic HPV (especially HPV 16 in the oropharynx) and EBV (in the nasopharynx). High-yield pearl: Head & Neck Malignancies: >90% Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC). Mucosal origin, linked to Tobacco + Alcohol (synergistic) and HPV-16 (Oropharynx: base of tongue, tonsils). Exam trap: HPV-positive oropharyngeal SCC has a significantly BETTER overall prognosis and response to chemoradiotherapy than HPV-negative (smoking-related) SCC.

optionExplanations.B: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common cutaneous cancer of the face/head/neck skin, but does not arise from mucosal aerodigestive surfaces.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Squamous cell carcinoma accounts for more than 90-95% of mucosal head and neck malignancies.
optionExplanations.D: Mucosal melanoma is an extremely rare, highly aggressive malignancy accounting for < 1% of sinonasal tumors.

It originates near the sphenopalatine foramen. The classic clinical presentation is recurrent, unprovoked, severe EPISTAXIS accompanied by progressive unilateral nasal obstruction. Its primary blood supply is derived from the internal maxillary artery (sphenopalatine branch). Surgical resection is the first-line definitive treatment, routinely preceded by preoperative transcatheter angiographic embolization within 24–48 hours to minimize intraoperative blood loss. High-yield pearl: Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA): Adolescent MALE + Recurrent severe epistaxis + Nasal obstruction. Origin: Sphenopalatine foramen. Blood supply: Internal Maxillary Artery. Management: Angiography + Embolization -> Endoscopic surgical resection. DO NOT BIOPSY in outpatient clinic! Exam trap: Never biopsy a suspected JNA in an outpatient setting; massive life-threatening hemorrhage will occur.

questions.question: Referred otalgia from tonsillar cancer is transmitted through:

questions.question: Which statement is wrong regarding the anterior neck triangle?
